title: Measurement, Units, Precision and Accuracy
purpose: Seed measurement semantics so Lantern represents quantities with units, uncertainty, instrument/method and scope, distinguishes accuracy from precision, and avoids false precision or invalid dimensional comparisons.

concepts.definition: A result produced by a defined procedure/instrument relating an observed property to a quantity/value under stated units and uncertainty.
A measurable property represented by a magnitude and quantity type, normally with a unit.
A defined reference scale used to express a quantity.
The physical or formal quantity dimension constraining meaningful unit conversion and algebra.
A semantics-preserving transformation between compatible units of the same quantity dimension.
A quantified or qualified range/distribution representing uncertainty attributable to the measurement process.
Closeness of a measurement/result to the relevant true/reference value, insofar as that value can be established.
Closeness/repeatability of repeated measurements or fineness of reported numerical resolution; high precision need not imply accuracy.
Smallest change or increment an instrument/procedure can meaningfully distinguish/report.
Comparison/adjustment of an instrument or procedure against appropriate reference standards.
A persistent directional or structured measurement bias not eliminated by repeated sampling alone.
Variation in repeated measurement arising from stochastic/uncontrolled influences.
Systematic deviation between expected measurement/estimate and target/reference under the applicable method.
Reported numerical detail justified by measurement resolution/uncertainty and subsequent computation.
A quantity computed from measured/input quantities under a declared relation, carrying propagated units and uncertainty.
Documented chain connecting a measurement/calibration to reference standards or procedures.

guards.reason: Repeatability/fine resolution does not establish closeness to truth/reference.
Measurements can center near a reference while individual results are widely dispersed.
Computation cannot create measurement information absent from inputs; propagation rules may further reduce justified precision.
Numerically similar values with incompatible dimensions are not equal measurements.
A magnitude without required unit/context is incomplete.
Resolution contributes to uncertainty but does not capture all error sources.
Repeated measurements can reduce random uncertainty but do not automatically correct systematic bias.
Calibration supplies evidence and traceability, not perfect measurement.
Unit conversion changes representation, not evidential quality.
Construct/measurement validity must establish that the instrument output represents the intended quantity.

invariants: A measurement should preserve value, unit/quantity type, method/instrument, scope and available uncertainty.
Numerical resolution and total uncertainty are distinct.
Units may be converted only across compatible dimensions using declared conversions.
A unit conversion changes representation, not evidence quality.
Repeated measurement reduces some random uncertainty but does not automatically remove systematic error.
Reported precision must not exceed what measurement and computation justify.
Calibration provides evidence about measurement performance and traceability, not infallibility.
Instrument output is not automatically a valid measurement of the intended construct.
Derived quantities preserve dimensional semantics and should propagate uncertainty.
Deterministic numerical code should perform conversions/error propagation where available; seed rules define meaning and constraints.

provenance.authoring_basis: Measurement science/metrology foundations, dimensional analysis and uncertainty principles adapted to Lantern's evidence and deterministic-computation architecture.
